analysis.one_liner: Requires farm equipment makers to sell repair parts, manuals, and tools to owners and independent shops.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote and died in the Senate Commerce Committee when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required manufacturers of electronics-enabled farm equipment, such as tractors and combines with onboard computers, to sell repair documentation, parts, software, and tools to equipment owners and independent repair shops on the same terms they give their own authorized dealers. It would also let people bypass digital locks that block repair, put patents and copyrights into the public domain if a manufacturer withholds required items, and let the Federal Trade Commission enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers and ranchers who own or lease modern equipment, and independent repair shops. Today, much farm equipment depends on embedded software, and owners often cannot fix a breakdown or even run diagnostics without going to an authorized dealer, which can mean waiting days during planting or harvest. The bill would let them buy the parts and tools to fix machines themselves or at a local shop, and would require free access to service documentation and software tools.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to offer owners and independent repair shops the parts, tools, documentation, and software needed to diagnose, maintain, or repair equipment on terms no worse than those given to authorized dealers, with documentation and software tools available at no charge [S3].

Bars manufacturers from requiring parts to be registered, paired, or approved by the manufacturer or a dealer before they will work, and bars imposing unnecessary costs or impediments on repairs [S3].

Allows circumvention of copyright-protected digital locks for repair, interoperability, and security research, and permits the trafficking in tools for those purposes, so owners are not blocked by software restrictions [S3].

If a manufacturer stops supplying a required item to authorized repair providers, any copyright or patent it holds on that item goes into the public domain, and it must require parts be replaceable without damage using commonly available tools [S3].
Enforcement is assigned to the Federal Trade Commission, treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of electronics-enabled farm equipment, such as makers of tractors and combines, would lose some control over and revenue from service, parts, and diagnostics, which are a significant profit center. Their authorized dealer networks would face competition from independent shops. Manufacturers argue repair access touches intellectual property, trade secrets, and safety, though the bill explicitly preserves trade secrets except where needed for repair and prohibits modifications that disable safety systems or evade emissions or safety laws [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Farm equipment manufacturers and their dealers

drawbacks.text: Equipment manufacturers would lose a lucrative service and parts business, and opponents argue that forcing disclosure of diagnostic software and repair processes risks exposing trade secrets and intellectual property, even though the bill contains an explicit carve-out that it does not require divulging trade secrets except as needed for repair access [S3].

Safety and emissions risks: allowing owners to modify software could lead to unsafe or non-compliant machines; the bill responds by prohibiting changes that disable safety notifications, bring equipment out of emissions or safety compliance, or violate law, but enforcement of those limits would depend on FTC rulemaking and case-by-case policing [S3].

The bill's key terms, such as 'fair and reasonable terms', would have to be defined through an FTC rulemaking process, which can take years and invite litigation, delaying any real-world benefit to farmers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for farmers: faster, cheaper repairs during narrow planting and harvest windows, and genuine ownership of equipment they have already paid for. The main costs fall on manufacturers and their dealers in the form of reduced service revenue and some exposure of proprietary repair processes, with the bill's trade-secret, safety, and emissions carve-outs addressing the strongest good-faith objections. The design is reasonably careful, though its reliance on FTC rulemaking would have slowed implementation.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Jon Tester introduced the bill on February 1, 2022, joined by Sen. Ben Ray Lujan [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the committee never scheduled a markup or vote, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
Only one senator cosponsored the bill, so it lacked the broad support needed to force committee action [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farm equipment manufacturers keep their exclusive control over parts, diagnostics, and service, so farmers still depend on authorized dealers for repairs. Independent repair shops remain shut out of much of that work.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farm equipment makers and dealer networks

for.name: Sen. Jon Tester
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Agricultural Right to Repair Act on February 1, 2022.

for.name: Sen. Ben Ray Lujan
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as its only cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill after referral; no markup, no vote, and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress.

against.name: Farm equipment manufacturers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed right-to-repair mandates covering their equipment, arguing repair access threatens intellectual property, cybersecurity, and safety.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, while the Republican and Democratic members of the Commerce Committee alike never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would strip manufacturers of exclusive control over repair parts, diagnostic software, and service manuals, which are a major profit center alongside machine sales. Farmers would be able to fix their own machines instead of returning to dealer-only service.

Dealers would lose a captive service market: independent shops and owners could buy parts and tools at the same prices and terms the manufacturer gives dealers. Dealer service revenue would face direct competition.

Shops would gain access to manuals, diagnostic tools, and parts at dealer-equivalent terms, letting them compete for repair work they are often currently locked out of. This runs alongside farmers' interest in faster, cheaper fixes.
Owners would get repair rights over machines they have bought, cutting repair costs and downtime during time-critical planting and harvest windows.
